title: Unique ID Generator
prompt: Every service in our company needs IDs for new rows, messages and events. Design a way to generate unique 64-bit IDs that roughly sort by creation time, across several data centers, without a central bottleneck.

clarify.q: Must the ID fit in 64 bits, or is 128 bits acceptable?
clarify.why: If 128 bits is fine, a time-ordered UUID solves the problem with no coordination at all. The 64-bit limit is what forces us to budget bits for time, machine and sequence.

clarify.q: How strictly must IDs be ordered: globally, per machine, or just roughly by time?
clarify.why: Strict global order needs a single sequencer or a consensus round per ID, which conflicts with 'no bottleneck'. Rough order within a few milliseconds is cheap.

clarify.q: What is the peak rate, overall and on the busiest single machine?
clarify.why: The busiest machine sets how many sequence bits we need per millisecond. The total sets nothing if generation is local.

clarify.q: How many machines and data centers will generate IDs, now and in 5 years?
clarify.why: This sets the machine-id bits. If autoscaling creates thousands of short-lived instances, ids must be leased and recycled rather than configured by hand.

clarify.q: How long must the scheme last?
clarify.why: The timestamp bits and the chosen epoch set the lifetime. 41 bits of milliseconds is about 70 years; fewer bits buy machine or sequence space but shorten it.

clarify.q: Is it acceptable that an ID reveals its creation time and roughly how many IDs we issue?
clarify.why: Time-ordered IDs leak creation time and approximate volume. For public-facing IDs such as order numbers that may be a business concern.

clarify.q: Do browsers or JavaScript clients consume these IDs?
clarify.why: JavaScript numbers are exact only up to 2⁵³, so 64-bit IDs must travel as strings in JSON or they get silently corrupted.

functional: Generate an ID that is unique across all services, machines and data centers, forever within the scheme's lifetime.
IDs fit in a signed 64-bit integer and are always positive.
IDs from one generator are strictly increasing; IDs from different generators are ordered by creation time to within the clock skew (target ≤ 10 ms).
Given an ID, any service can decode its creation time, region and worker without a lookup.
Work keeps going when other data centers or the coordination service are unreachable.
nonFunctional: Generation is local: p99 under 1 µs in-process, no network call per ID.
Sustain 1 M IDs/s on one worker; total demand of 2 M IDs/s at peak across the company.
Zero duplicates, including across restarts, clock adjustments and failovers. A duplicate is a data-corruption bug.
Lifetime of at least 60 years from the chosen epoch.
Up to 4 096 concurrent generators across up to 16 regions.
outOfScope: Human-friendly short codes (such as order numbers on receipts), which can be derived from IDs separately.
Gap-free sequences, such as invoice numbers that legally must be consecutive. Those need a transactional counter.
Hiding creation time from outsiders. We note it as a trade-off, not a requirement.

assumptions: 64 bits total: 1 sign bit + 41 bits timestamp (ms) + 4 bits region + 8 bits worker + 10 bits sequence
Custom epoch 2026-01-01, so we do not waste bits on years since 1970
2 M IDs/s at peak company-wide, from about 2 000 processes
The busiest single process issues up to 50 000 IDs/s in bursts
NTP keeps clocks within about 10 ms of each other

steps.label: Bit budget
steps.result: Fits a signed 64-bit integer; the top bit stays 0 so IDs are positive

steps.label: Per-worker capacity
steps.result: ≈ 1.02 M IDs/s per worker, 20× the busiest process

steps.label: Fleet capacity vs demand
steps.result: About 1 000× headroom; capacity is not the constraint, uniqueness is

steps.label: Index savings vs 128-bit UUIDs
steps.math: 8 bytes saved per key × 10 B rows ≈ 80 GB per index that stores the key
steps.result: Smaller, denser B-tree indexes and foreign keys

estimates.takeaway:
Throughput is a non-problem: 1 M IDs/s per worker against a busiest-process need of 50 000/s. The hard parts are elsewhere: giving each of up to 4 096 generators a unique worker slot, and never issuing a duplicate when a clock jumps backwards. That is where the deep dives go.

The 69.7-year lifetime holds only if we pick a recent epoch. Starting from 1970 would have already used 56 of those years.

api.note: In-process, lock-free per worker. Blocks for under 1 ms if the 1 024 per-ms sequence is exhausted.
Pure function, used in debugging and to route by creation time.
For languages or serverless functions that cannot hold a worker lease. IDs are returned as strings so JavaScript does not round them.
How a process claims its worker slot at startup and keeps it with a keep-alive every 10 s.

entities.name: WorkerSlot
entities.store: etcd (one key per slot, attached to a 30 s lease), one etcd cluster per region
fields: slot is freed when the lease expires
entities.why: Guarantees no two live processes in a region hold the same worker number. Regions do not need to coordinate because the region id is part of the ID.

entities.name: LastIssued checkpoint
entities.store: Local disk file per process, plus a field in the WorkerSlot value
entities.why: Lets a restarted process refuse to issue IDs with timestamps it may already have used, even if the clock moved back while it was down.

data.note: There is almost no data. The design is a bit layout plus a lease. The only shared store is etcd, holding at most 256 tiny keys per region. It is touched at startup and by keep-alives every 10 s, never per ID. If etcd is down, running processes keep issuing IDs on their current lease until it would expire, and new processes cannot start generating.

hld.summary:
Generation happens inside each service process through a small library, so producing an ID is a few CPU instructions: read the clock, compare with the last timestamp, bump the sequence, shift and OR the parts together. There is no network hop and no shared bottleneck.

Uniqueness comes from the layout. Two processes can produce the same timestamp and sequence, but never with the same (region, worker) pair. The region id is fixed per data center in config. The worker id is leased from etcd in that region at startup and kept alive while the process lives. Each host runs NTP (or the cloud provider's time sync) to keep clocks close, which gives the rough global ordering. For callers that cannot hold a lease, such as short-lived serverless functions, a tiny ID service uses the same library and hands out batches over HTTP.

flows.title: Process start-up
steps: Read region id (0–15) from deployment config.
Grant a 30 s lease in the regional etcd and try put-if-absent on /idgen/{region}/{w} for w = random start, scanning until a free slot is found.
Read the slot's previous lastTimestamp. If the local clock is behind it, wait until the clock passes it (or refuse to start if the gap is over 5 s).
Start keep-alives every 10 s. Only then mark the process ready for traffic.

flows.title: Generating one ID
steps: now = current time in ms − epoch.
If now == last: sequence = (sequence + 1) mod 1 024; if it is back at this millisecond's starting value, all 1 024 are used, so spin until the next millisecond.
If now > last: sequence = 0 (or a small random start to spread low bits), last = now.
If now < last: the clock went backwards. Handle as in the clock deep dive.

flows.title: Lease lost
steps: Keep-alives fail (network split from etcd) and the lease approaches expiry.
At 25 s without a successful keep-alive, before the 30 s TTL, the library stops issuing IDs and returns errors.
The process marks itself unhealthy, so the load balancer drains it, and it re-acquires a slot when etcd is back.

deepDives.title: Which scheme at all
deepDives.problem: Several well-known approaches give unique IDs. They differ in size, ordering, coordination and failure behaviour, and interviewers want to see the 64-bit constraint drive the choice rather than a reflexive 'use Snowflake'.

options.name: Random UUID (version 4)
options.how: 122 random bits from a secure random source, generated anywhere.
pros: Zero coordination, no clocks
Unguessable, reveals nothing
cons: 128 bits breaks the 64-bit requirement
Random order scatters inserts across the whole B-tree, causing page splits and poor cache locality on big tables
No time ordering

options.name: Time-ordered UUID (version 7)
options.how: 48 bits of ms timestamp followed by random bits, 128 bits total.
pros: No coordination and no worker ids
Sorts by time, so inserts land at the right edge of indexes
A standard format with growing library support
cons: Still 128 bits
Order within the same millisecond across machines is random

options.name: Database sequence or ticket server
options.how: A dedicated database hands out numbers, or each app reserves a block of 1 000 at a time.
pros: Dense, small numbers
Strict order inside one server
cons: Central dependency on the write path: if it is down, nobody creates rows
Multi-region needs interleaving tricks (odd/even, offsets) or a cross-region call
Block reservation breaks time ordering across blocks

options.name: Time + region + worker + sequence in 64 bits
options.how: Pack a ms timestamp, a region id, a leased worker id and a per-ms counter into one integer, generated in-process.
pros: Fits 64 bits and sorts roughly by time
No network call per ID; works during partitions
Decodable for debugging
cons: Depends on clocks behaving; needs a clock-backwards policy
Needs worker-id leasing, which is the main operational risk
Leaks creation time and volume

deepDives.choice:
Time + region + worker + sequence, in-process. The 64-bit requirement rules out UUIDs, and 'no central bottleneck across data centers' rules out a sequence server. The packed layout is the only option that meets both.

What would change my mind: if 128 bits were acceptable, I would use UUIDv7 and delete the worker-lease system entirely. The extra 8 bytes per key cost about 80 GB per index over 10 B rows, which is often cheaper than running etcd leases correctly.

diagram.title: Bit layout of one ID
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  A["sign - 1 bit - always 0"] --> B["timestamp - 41 bits - ms since 2026-01-01"]
  B --> C["region - 4 bits - 16 regions"]
  C --> D["worker - 8 bits - 256 per region"]
  D --> E["sequence - 10 bits - 1024 per ms"]

deepDives.title: Spending the 63 usable bits
deepDives.problem: Every bit given to one field halves another. The layout is a commitment we cannot easily change once IDs are stored everywhere, so each field's size must come from the numbers.

options.name: Wide sequence, narrow machine field (41 / 10 machine / 12 sequence)
options.how: 1 024 machines, 4 096 IDs per ms per machine.
pros: 4 M IDs/s per machine
Suits a few large central ID servers
cons: 1 024 machine slots is tight when every app process generates its own IDs and autoscaling churns instances
We would never use 4 M/s per process

options.name: Balanced (41 / 4 region + 8 worker / 10 sequence)
options.how: 16 regions × 256 workers = 4 096 generators, 1 024 IDs per ms each.
pros: Matches our numbers: 2 000 processes now, 1 M/s per process vs 50 000 needed
Region bits allow independent per-region leasing with no global coordination
cons: 256 workers per region caps one region at 256 concurrent generator processes
A seventeenth region needs a new layout

options.name: Coarser time (seconds or 10 ms ticks)
options.how: Use fewer time bits and give the rest to workers or sequence.
pros: Much longer lifetime or many more workers
cons: Ordering within a tick is lost across machines
The sequence must cover a whole tick, so a busy worker needs more sequence bits anyway

deepDives.choice:
Balanced: 41 / 4 / 8 / 10. Our pressure is the number of generators, not the rate per generator. 10 sequence bits still gives 20× the busiest process's burst rate.

What would change my mind: if one region grows past about 200 generator processes, I would move generation for low-volume services to the regional ID service (batches over HTTP), so worker slots go only to high-volume services. If that is not enough, take 2 bits from sequence (256 IDs per ms is still 256 000/s) to get 1 024 workers per region. Changing the layout is safe only if the new IDs stay larger than all old IDs and stay unique, so planning the bits up front is far cheaper.

deepDives.title: Assigning worker ids
deepDives.problem: Two live processes with the same (region, worker) will eventually create identical IDs. That is silent data corruption. Containers start and die constantly, so worker ids cannot be hand-assigned.

options.name: Static config per host
options.how: Each host gets a worker number in its deployment config.
pros: No dependency at runtime
cons: Copy-paste errors produce duplicates
Breaks with autoscaling and several processes per host

options.name: Derive from IP address or host name
options.how: Use the low 8 bits of the private IP.
pros: Automatic, no coordination
cons: Two hosts in different subnets can share low bits
IP reuse after a quick restart can overlap with the old process still draining

options.name: Lease from a coordination service
options.how: Claim a slot in etcd or ZooKeeper with put-if-absent tied to a TTL lease, keep it alive, and stop issuing before the lease can expire.
pros: Uniqueness backed by a consensus store
Slots return to the pool automatically when processes die
Easy to see who holds what
cons: Another system to run, one per region
The process must stop issuing when it cannot renew, which needs careful timing

deepDives.choice:
Lease from etcd, per region. The safety rule is about timing: the process stops issuing IDs 5 s before its lease could expire (25 s into a 30 s TTL without a renewal). Then even if etcd hands the slot to someone else at 30 s, the two never issue at the same time. A paused process (long GC, frozen VM) is the edge case. It checks the lease time before every batch of issues, using a monotonic clock, and refuses if the lease is stale.

What would change my mind: a small, fixed fleet (say 20 VMs that rarely change). Then static config with a startup check that the slot is not already advertised is simpler and has no runtime dependency.

deepDives.title: When the clock goes backwards
deepDives.problem: NTP may step a clock back after a bad sync, a VM may migrate to a host with a different clock, and leap seconds may be applied by repeating a second. If our timestamp goes back by 3 ms, we will reuse (timestamp, sequence) pairs we already issued, and those IDs are duplicates.

options.name: Ignore it
pros: Simplest
cons: Produces real duplicates after every backwards step. Never acceptable.

options.name: Wait it out for small jumps, fail for large ones
options.how: If now < last by up to 5 ms, spin until the clock passes last. If by more, stop issuing, raise an alert and mark the process unhealthy.
pros: Never duplicates
Small jumps cost a few ms of latency, which is invisible
cons: A big step takes the process out of service until a human or the clock catches up
Needs the alerting to be real

options.name: Logical clock: keep using last
options.how: If now < last, keep timestamp = last and keep incrementing the sequence. When the sequence wraps, advance the timestamp by 1 ms on our own.
pros: No stalls, always available
Still strictly increasing per worker
cons: Our timestamps drift ahead of real time while the wall clock catches up, which hurts ordering across machines
A long drift makes decoded times wrong

deepDives.choice:
Combine: run time sync in slewing mode so it adjusts gradually instead of stepping, use a leap-second smear, wait out jumps of up to 5 ms, use the logical-clock trick for jumps of up to 1 s, and fail closed beyond that. The checkpointed lastTimestamp covers the restart case: a process that comes back with a clock behind its own last issued timestamp waits or refuses to start.

What would change my mind: environments with bounded-uncertainty clocks (some clouds expose a clock with an error bound). Then the generator can wait out the uncertainty window and offer tighter cross-machine ordering.

failures: Two processes end up with the same worker id (a lease bug or a frozen VM wakes up)
Stop issuing before lease expiry with a monotonic-clock check. Add a background job that samples recent IDs per (region, worker) from logs and alerts if two hosts report the same pair.
NTP steps the clock back 2 seconds on one host
The generator refuses to issue, the host goes unhealthy, the load balancer drains it, and on-call is paged. No duplicates are created.
Regional etcd is down for 10 minutes

Running processes keep issuing as long as their leases are valid. Leases cannot be renewed, so processes stop at 25 s, and the region stops creating rows. Run etcd as 5 nodes across 3 zones, and give leases a longer TTL (5 min) with a correspondingly earlier stop, if that trade is acceptable.
Always serialize IDs as strings in JSON APIs. Add a contract test that sends an ID above 2⁵³ through every public endpoint.
A busy process exhausts 1 024 IDs in one millisecond
The generator spins to the next millisecond: a short stall, not an error. Alert if spins exceed 1% of calls, which means the service needs more workers or a wider sequence.
scale: 10× processes (20 000): slots run out at 4 096. Move low-volume services to the regional ID service that hands out batches, so only about 500 heavy services hold leases, or switch to a new layout with more worker bits and a versioned epoch.
10× rate per process (500 000/s): still under the 1 M/s cap. Use one generator per thread with separate worker slots to avoid contention on one atomic counter.
More than 16 regions: plan a layout version early. A common trick is to change the epoch when the layout changes, so new IDs still sort after old ones.

followups.q: Why not just use the database's auto-increment?
answer: It works on one primary, but then every insert in every service depends on that primary, and failover can reuse or skip numbers if not configured carefully.
With shards or regions you must interleave (shard k issues k, k+N, …), which breaks time order across shards and makes adding a shard painful.
We often need the ID before the insert, for example to publish an event or link child rows in one batch.

followups.q: Can someone learn how many orders we get per day from our IDs?
answer: Yes, roughly: the timestamp gives the creation time, and if sequence numbers start at 0 each millisecond, sampling IDs leaks volume.
Mitigate by starting each millisecond's sequence at a random offset, and by exposing a separate opaque public ID (random or encrypted) for customer-facing objects.
Keep the 64-bit ID internal for joins and indexes.

followups.q: Two events happened in different regions. Can we trust ID order to tell us which was first?
answer: Only to within the clock skew, about 10 ms with NTP. Inside that window the order is arbitrary.
For causal order (a reply must sort after its message), include the parent's ID and make the child's timestamp max(now, parentTimestamp + 1).
For strict global order, you need a single sequencer per ordering domain, for example per chat or per account.

followups.q: How do you use these IDs as a database shard key?
answer: Do not range-shard on the raw ID: all new writes go to the shard holding the newest range, which makes it a hot spot.
Hash the ID to choose a shard, or shard by a business key such as customerId and use the ID only as the row key.
Time-ordered IDs are still great inside a shard, because inserts append to the right edge of the B-tree.
The 41-bit timestamp overflows into the sign bit and IDs go negative, breaking ordering.
Plan a layout version with a new epoch well before then, and alert when less than 10 years remain.
The cheap insurance is documenting the epoch and layout next to the code.

mistakes: Using the Unix epoch, which wastes 56 of the 69.7 years of a 41-bit millisecond timestamp before the first ID.
Saying 'use the IP address as worker id' without addressing reuse and collisions.
Ignoring clock-backwards behaviour, the single most likely source of duplicates.
Proposing a central ID service called on every insert, then needing a cache, then a cluster: rebuilding the bottleneck the question asked to avoid.
Forgetting that JavaScript cannot represent 64-bit integers exactly, so IDs break in the frontend.

Gave a concrete clock-backwards policy with thresholds
